paras: The Berkley poll-tax riot took place on the night of December 8, 1903, when about 300 armed white "straightout" Democrats in Berkley, Norfolk County, Virginia, drove county officials and a group of Black men from an office where the men had come to pay their poll taxes. The crowd kicked County Treasurer Samuel W. Lyons down a flight of stairs and choked County Clerk Alvah H. Martin, the Fusionist leader; shots were fired, but no one was reported hit. The Richmond Times-Dispatch called it a "Party Riot," and the Richmond Planet condemned it as a "high-handed proceeding" against Black taxpayers.

Under Virginia's new suffrage law a voter had to pay his poll tax to qualify, and Norfolk County's tax offices were held by the Fusionists, whom the New-York Tribune described as Democrats, Republicans and Black voters. The straightout Democrats complained that "political dodges" kept them from paying their taxes while Black voters were allowed to pay surreptitiously. According to the New York Sun, they learned on December 8 that Fusionist voters, "consisting chiefly of negroes," could pay at George Martin's office in Berkley.

That night a church bell summoned the straightouts, and a crowd the wire put at 300 white men, nearly all armed, gathered at the building where Lyons was receiving taxes. Inside were Lyons, other county and town officials and "nearly a score of negroes" by the wire's count, a dozen by the Times-Dispatch's. The crowd forced everyone into the street, kicking Lyons halfway down the stairs.

It then pushed past the police at the Berkley police station and seized Martin, who was meeting there with the Rev. John Sumler, a Black councilman. Martin was choked and held against a cell door while three men, named by the Times-Dispatch as Clarence McCoy, W. H. Groves and R. Moore, lectured him, and the correspondent wrote that "at one time it was feared that murder might be done." Police restored order and escorted Martin home; several shots fired in the street hit no one. Two short dispatches added that Black residents were driven from the streets into the "negro quarter" at shotgun point.

Warrants were reported issued for the station-house attackers, but the next day the Times-Dispatch wrote that no arrests had been made, and it carried the straightouts' defense, which the Fusionists denied. Troops were mentioned but, by the Virginia paper's account, not needed. On December 11 a Tribune telegram called a bloody clash "inevitable," reported the Fusionists arming, and quoted a Berkley mass meeting pledging "our fortunes, our lives and our honor" against Fusionist "lawlessness." No report of an indictment or trial was found; in January 1904 the Planet wrote that no arrests had yet been made and the matter seemed "treated lightly in official circles."

Most white papers framed the episode as a quarrel between white factions centered on the assaulted officials. The long wire, run as "Mobbed by Democrats" in Indianapolis and reprinted in Birmingham, Gainesville and Mitchell, South Dakota, repeated the Democrats' charge of surreptitious poll-tax collection from Black voters. Headlines assigned the racial stakes variously: "Republican Fusion With Negroes" (Birmingham), "Negro Office Holders" (Gainesville), "Because He Registered Negro Voters" (Omaha) and "Mob Drives Off Negroes" (New York Sun). The Richmond Times-Dispatch, with a Norfolk correspondent, called it a "Party Riot" and then "Shot-Gun Politics."

The Richmond Planet treated the riot as an assault on Black citizens' rights. Its editorial "Trouble at Berkley" described the Black taxpayers as "property owners, thrifty and responsible," driven off with shotguns while "on a peaceful mission," and warned that "a flock of sheep will never do to meet a drove of wolves." It returned to the case in January 1904, though it then named the threatened treasurer "MARTIN."

Injuries differ by source: the wire and Times-Dispatch say Lyons was kicked and Martin choked, the Sun that Martin was "seriously hurt" and many of the mob injured, and the Stark County Democrat that both were "badly beaten." The Planet said the treasurer took refuge in the station house, whereas the wire and the local correspondent place Martin there.

reader.title: Berkley poll-tax riot
bases: An armed crowd of white Democrats drove Black men from an office where they had come to pay the poll taxes that qualified them to vote, and assaulted the white Fusionist officials receiving them; shots were fired but no one was reported hit (A1, A6, A15).

The wire report (A1), the Richmond Times-Dispatch's Norfolk correspondent (A6), the New York Sun (A5) and the Richmond Planet (A15) independently agree that armed straightout Democrats drove officials and Black taxpayers from the tax office in Berkley on December 8.

accounts.label: Wire report (Norfolk)
accounts.gist: A mob of 300 armed white Democrats stormed the improvement board office, ejected officials and about a score of Black men, kicked Lyons, then choked Martin at the police station; the cause was factional feeling and the Democrats' charge of surreptitious poll-tax collection from Black voters.

accounts.label: Times-Dispatch Norfolk correspondent
accounts.gist: Straightouts who said they were being disfranchised summoned friends by church bell, assaulted Lyons at the Martin building, broke past police to attack Martin; murder was feared; warrants issued, but no arrests the next day.

accounts.label: New York Sun dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of straightouts drove Fusionists and Black taxpayers from George Martin's office; Alvah H. Martin was thrown down and seriously hurt and many of the mob were injured.

accounts.label: Short wire
accounts.gist: Democrats drove Lyons out for registering Black voters and forced Black residents into one section (the 'negro quarter') at shotgun point; troops might be called.

accounts.label: Straightouts' justification
accounts.gist: White voters had been exasperated by obstacles to paying their poll taxes while Black voters had everything made easy; the Fusionists denied it.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: Lawless armed Democrats drove Black men from the treasurer's office at gunpoint while they were lawfully paying poll taxes; the treasurer had to take refuge in the station house and no arrests followed.

framing.detail: The long wire ran as 'Mobbed by Democrats', 'Democratic Mob Assaults County Officers' and 'Mob of Politicians', centered on the assaulted officials and the Democrats' charge.
The Richmond Times-Dispatch called it a 'Party Riot' and 'Shot-Gun Politics', reported the attack in detail and gave the straightouts' defense.

Heads and briefs named race: 'Mob Drives Off Negroes' (Sun), 'Because He Registered Negro Voters' (Omaha Bee), 'Race Riot' (Stark County Democrat), 'White Men Mob Negro Office Holders' (Gainesville Star).
The Richmond Planet's 'Trouble at Berkley' denounced the 'lawless elements', noted no arrests and urged Black residents to stand for their rights.
